ONE HITCH
TALE OF A LABEL

Counsel On A "Master
Forgery."

The action of a cashier in refusing to have anything further to do with an account in which there had been large deposits and equally large withdrawals in the course of a few days led to what Mr. F. C. Jenkins described at the Sessions this morning as the one hitch which led to the prevention of a "master forgery" against which the Wing On Bank would have had no answer.

The facts which he was going to prove, said Mr. Jenkin, prosecuting, were that the two prisoners conspired together in getting two deposit books from the Wing. On Company which was an emporium which in common with others had been given power by the Ordinances to run a banking business.
Having deposited $50,000 in one of the books, alleged Mr. Jenkin, they removed the distinctive outside label with its number and put it on the other which presumably they had got on the minimum deposit of $100, making forgeries of certain items in the first book, thus getting their money back.

If the parties to the conspiracy had been only able to get back the book and its genuine label, said Mr. Jenkin, the Wing On Bang would have had no option but to pay out again: the $50,000, for the original book had blank withdrawal pages and the amount of $50,000 in deposit.

The Bank; however, continued Mr. Jenkin, had a rule that all books from which all deposits had been entirely removed, should revert the Bank's own property. Knowing this, the conspirators arranged to take out all but $1,000 of the amount of $50,000.they had put in.

"But the unfortunate part, from their point of view," continued Mr. Jenkin, was that the cashier who had the handling of this account, on seeing that out of $50,000, $49,000 had been removed in a few days, told the bearer of the book that the Wing On Company did not want an account of that nature; that it was no use to them and that the depositors would have to withdraw the whole amount."
"Not Without Humour."

“So one has a situation which was not without its amusing side; in spite of the seriousness of the issue,” continued counsel. “Here was a man who wanted the label on that book above all things, deprived of that label because of the Bank’s unalterable practice of taking the book once the account was closed.”

Reverting to the book which had been originally used for the deposit of the $50,000, counsel produced dummy copies which were given to His Lordship other counsel and the jury illustrating what he (Mr. Jenkin) alleged to have been the methods used by the conspirators.

Mr. Jenkin said that he was going to call scientific men with scientific apparatus to show, when this new complication arose in the arrangement of the conspirators, they forged another label also as to the methods used in the alteration of the second deposit book taken to the bank for the withdrawals.

Counsel caused much amusement by stating that the confusion which had arisen at the Magistracy as to the naming of the two books involved would necessitate him, with His Lordship's permission, if he did not think it was too frivolous, calling the two books "Emma" and "Nina".

In accordance with court practice, the exhibits in the case had been named alphabetically in the order of their appearance and the two books in question had, in that order to be called "N" and "N". This had led to much phonetic misunderstanding and the suggestion of "Emma" and "Nina" was the only alternative.
(Continued at foot of next Column.)
WILFUL DAMAGE.
ACCUSED ABSENT.

Jones Brown, engineman of the U.S.A. "Helena" was not present at the Central Magistracy this morning to answer a charge of causing willful damage to furniture to the extent of $100 at a Japanese house in Wanchai yesterday.
It was explained by Divisional Inspector Ogg that the usual procedure of handing over the man to an escort from the ship had been adopted and in the meantime the vessel had left port on a temporary absence.
The Magistrate (Mr. Lindsell), thought that bail to cover damage done in such cases should be asked for and adjourned hearing for one week.
INSPECTION POSTPONED.
The inspection of the Hongkong Police by His Excellency the Governor, arranged for this afternoon, has had to be again postponed for one week at the last moment owing to the bad weather.

“Nina” was the exhibit model of the book which counsel alleged the conspirators had got by the deposit of the minimum $100 which the Bank required and Mr. Jenkin was responsible for smiles in court when he said that “Nina” was perfectly genuine except for the label whereas “Emma” was an out and out forgery and a master one at that.

Detecting Forgery Methods
Mr. Jenkin said that the case would provide the jury with some interesting material. If they learnt nothing as to what they might consider, actual forgery he could promise them they would learn something about the methods of detecting forgery and this case involved not only forgery of printing matter and chops but of the actual handwriting of the principals required to sign in these transactions. The case was not only important from the banking point of view but also from the general commercial standpoint.

Included in the charges of conspiracy to defraud, were indictments against the first prisoner (Au Kim-lui) of perjury in connection with his evidence in a Supreme Court action in which he stated that the Wing On Bank were indebted to him for the $50,000 originally deposited.
Mr. Alabaster's Point
Before the charges were read out at this morning's proceedings, Mr. C. G. Alabaster, K.C., made an application before the second prisoner (Lam Fuk-chiu) was called upon to plead.

Mr. Alabaster pointed out that the two prisoners had been charged on the same indictment where as from the particulars as set out by the prosecution it was clear that the second prisoner was not charged with perjury. He moved that either the indictment be quashed or with the alternatives that the two last counts referring to the alleged perjury be struck out or that the prosecution be called on to elect which counts they would proceed with. Mr. Alabaster pointed out the anomalies of prisoner being called upon to plead on a count on which he was not charged.

Mr. Jenkin pointed out that the same facts in the conspiracy charge stood for the perjury charge and after cases had been quoted and some legal argument, His Lordship held that he did not see any ground for alleging that the second prisoner would be aeriously embarrassed by the inclusion in the indictment of those two counts. He did not, at any rate, propose at that moment to exercise his discretion in favour of striking out the counts or hearing the case separately, although if, as the case proceeded, he should see reason, he might exercise his discretion.
Mr. F. C. Jenkin (together with Mr. Sheldon) was for the prosecution; Mr. C. G. Alabaster, K. C. for one prisoner and Mr. Elaley Zettlyn for the other.
The case is proceeding
MISSION GOODS.
CLERGYMAN'S KEROSINE

As the commodity is under a Canton Government monopoly, a quantity of kerosine oil for a foreign up-puntry mission formed the subject of a "seizure" on April 17 which, however, did not result in any complication.

For about a year, kerosine oil has been sold under the control of the Canton Government, this phase of what has been an extensive foreign trade having been reviewed in the last annual report of the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce.

As the tow-boat for Shekki was about to leave the Bund at Canton on the night of April 17, a party of plain-clothes searchers from the "Merchants' Protection Preventive Committee," accompanied by police, executed a search-warrant and detained 45 cases of kerosine oil on board without the revenue stamps attached.

A foreign clergyman who claimed to be associated with a mission at Shekkf (the vernacular report does not give any other detail as to the gentleman's identity) then came forward and explained that the oil was purchased in Canton for the poor in his district.

During the discussion a Chinese is alleged to have interceded on the clergyman's behalf. This man is described as the chief commissariat officer of General Li Fook-lam's army but his name is not given in the report.

When the chief of the Preventive Committee arrived on the scene, a permit was shown to him, issued by Mr. T. V. Soong, who is head of the Government monopoly. The mit was accepted and the oil was allowed to be shipped away. The so-called military officer is said to have tendered an apology for unwarranted interference, this being accepted.

People's Mass Protest.
From Ko. In comes news of a demonstration, which practically amounted to a riot, against the existence of the monopoly.
On April 15, over 10,000 people are said to have organised a parade. In spite of heavy rain, they marched to the local Government oil depot to protest, forcing an entrance.

The authorities, however, were prepared, police and military having assembled there. A number alleged to be leaders of the demonstrators were arrested.
The crowd then surrounded the depot until those detained had been released. One of the conditions of release was the setting off of firecrackers, this being a Chinese custom of restoration of "face."
WEST POINT SMASH.
TRAM AND ROLLER IN COLLISION.
YESTERDAY'S ACCIDENT
A collision took place yesterday morning between a P.W.D. motor roller and a tram car at Des Vœux Road West, near Whitty Street, the roller receiving the worst of the damage.

The driver of the tram, ear noticed the obstruction and the signal of the roller man to stop, but he stated to the police that the brakes did not hold owing to the slippery nature of the track.
Considerable damage was done to the water tank and tool box at the rear of the roller, but the driver was not hurt.
UNSAFE BUILDINGS.

The inmates of three houses (Nos. 209, 211, 213), Queen's Road West hurriedly vacated the premises yesterday when it was pointed out by officers from the P.W.D. that a collapse would take place at any moment.
Shoring operations began immediately the premises were vacated.
Pleading guilty to a charge of being found in a drunk and incapable condition at Arsenal Street, an unemployed seaman named James Ronan was fined $5 at the Central Magistracy this
CANTON LABOUR.
MERCHANTS FLOUTED.
Canton merchants are now reported to be in communication with the Provincial Government in regard to the suggested removal of all "strikers" to Whampoa.
Last week specific instances were mentioned in which so-called armed labour pickets marched into business premises and took possession whilst the Police remained inactive.

This interference, alleged to have originated in disputes between masters and their employees' guilds, is regarded very seriously. To-day the vernacular papers record another case of workmen taking the law into their own hands, ignoring the representatives of law and order.
The proposal that all strikers be accommodated at Whampoa in matsheds is mentioned as having been disfavoured by the labour leaders. On the other hand, the Canton merchants are said to have put forward statements that the labourers should not be allowed in the city, their presence being looked upon in the same light as the unruly military elements of the past.
MORE THAN $5.
ARRESTS FOR EXPORTING MONEY.
AN "ARMY" OFFENDER.

Important among the daily prosecutions for attempting to take away from the Colony more than the money allowed by the regulation were two cases before Mr. R.E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning.

Mr. E. S. C. Brooks, defending in one case, said that the accused was an officer attached to certain forces of General Chan Kwingming which suffered a reverse last year. While in Shanghai, accused heard that several subordinate officers had taken refuge in Macao, and he was now on his way to join them. Mr. Brooks submitted that the accused was ignorant of the regulation and had no intention of flouting the law.
The sum found on the accused amounting to $1,520, he was fined $100, the rest of the money to be returned to him.
A similar fine to be deducted from a sum of $1,140 was imposed on an educated Chinese, an emigrant returning from South America. It was stated that the money was found inside a cigarette packet.
CYCLE FATALITY
EUROPEAN MOTORIST IN COURT.
SERIOUS CHARGES

Charges of manslaughter and reckless driving were preferred against Mr. S. J. Squire at the Central Magistracy this morning when Mr. J. A. Gordon Leask appeared for the defence.
Applying for one week's formal remand, Sub-Inspector Alexander recalled an incident which occurred at the Causeway Bay junction on Saturday morning when two motor cycles were proceeding in the direction of the town. He said that one motor cycle took Caroline Road while the other (driven by Mr. Squirr) ran near the tram shelter and knocked down a Chinese who was standing there injuring him seriously and resulting in his death in hospital shortly afterwards.
Hearing was adjourned for one week.

Two Chinese charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with possession of daggers were remanded until to-morrow.
Thefts of awnings and rope valued at $90 from the steam launch "Lee On" and an awning valued at $140 from the steam launch "Man Hing" while lying at the water front yesterday have been reported to the police.

"DOLLAR" SHIPS: FURTHER
DETAILS
PRESIDENT BOATS SALE

Last Saturday it was published locally that a bid of G$8,000,000 by the Dollar interests had probably been accepted by the U.S. Shipping Board for the five "President" boats at present operated by the Admiral Oriental Line between Seattle and the Far East.
The figure is wrong, the error being due to the lack of full details in the message to the Hong Kong office.

The "Manila Bulletin" of April 15 throws further light on this great deal in tonnage. Although the Hongkong office has received no further information, an opinion has been expressed (by one of the local officials), that the Manila report is nearer the mark.
Extracts from the report are given below. Readers of the "China Mail" can read "Hong-kong" instead of "Manila" as the facts can apply to both ports of call. Says the "Bulletin"

The offer of $4,500,000 made by R. Stanley Dollar, representing the Dollar interests, for the five Admiral Oriental Liners being operated between Manila and Seattle by the United States Shipping Board, has been definitely accepted by the Shipping Board according to a cablegram received on April 14 by H. M. Cavender, general agent for the Dollar line.
The five liners that will join their sister ships belonging to the Dollar interests, are, the "Presidents McKinley, Jefferson, Grant, Madison and Jackson." These ships have been operated by the Dollar line for some time.
This makes three Dollar services coming to Manila, the found-the-world fleet, the San Francisco-Manila vessels and the Seattle-Oriental liners.

Three Bids In All
The bid of $4,500,000 made by the Dollar interest, was the third made before being accepted by the Shipping Board. This was an increase of $1,500,000 over the second bid, and at the time it was made a few weeks ago, it was understood that it would be accepted.
The second bid made by the Dollar people was $3,000,000, but the Shipping Board turned it down, not only on account of what they thought was a very low bid, but due to the Dollar interests' refusal to comply with the Shipping Board's stipulation, that the company put up a bond of $1,000,000 as a guarantee that they would maintain the ships in question on their present route, for five years. Although the cablegram received by Mr. Cavender did not state the terms of the sale, it is believed that the Dollar interests accepted the five year stipulation.

The sale of the five Admiral-Oriental liners to the Dollar interests now gives the latter monopoly on the American trans-Pacific passenger liner trade. A bitter fight to prevent the Dollar interests from buying these liners, was waged by Senator Jones of Washington, who believed that the Dollar Line would buy the liners, comply with the five year stipulation and then remove them from the Manila-Seattle run, owing to the heavy competition waged by British and Japanese interests.
Only one other bid was made for the five liners, $4,000,000 being offered by W. B. Keene, former vice-president of the Emergency Fleet Corporation, who represented the corporation in Seattle.
Where Others Failed.
A group of Seattle business men opposed the sale of the five ships to the Dollar interests. Recently this group requested permission to operate the five Admiral-Oriental liners, according to the United Press. Several members of the Shipping Board supported this project, as the best way to avoid creating a monopoly of the trans-Pacific shipping in the hands of one company. This offer was considered on April 14, but evidently the majority of the Shipping Board voted in favour of accepting the Dollar bid.
[The President Harding] and the President Roosevelt are the only remaining liners of the 535 type, now being operated by the United States Shipping Board. These air on the trans-Atlantic run
